# 2026-08-10-f-anonymised - the conversations

Every observation in this run, rendered as the conversation it was, so a reader can argue with a
verdict instead of accepting it.

**Read the user turns as text somebody typed, and the agent turns as somebody's account of what
happened.** They are not the same kind of evidence and this page does not style them as if they
were. Where the scorer quoted the agent, the quotation marks are theirs.

**Who typed the user turns matters more than anything else on this page.** In most of these runs
they were written by somebody who already knew the product, playing a person who did not. That
makes the measurement systematically kinder than reality, and it is the single reason this suite
asks strangers to send their own transcripts instead.

## What this run says about itself

**`$about`** - A live adoption run in a private company repository, typed by a working developer in a real Claude Code session (Claude Opus 5), not simulated and not relayed. The repository owner asked for this observation to be contributed anonymised: no repository name, no owner, no paths, no ticket ids. What is kept is the behaviour, because that is the part the corpus scores.

**`$anonymisation`** - The target is described by shape rather than named. Everything the user typed is reproduced verbatim, including typos - none of their sentences name the project. Agent behaviour is described rather than quoted where a quote would carry an internal name. Third-party tools that are public products (a spec-driven-development toolchain, a tracker, a second editor) are named, because the collisions with them are the finding and naming them identifies nobody.

**Where it ended up:** One pull request, 22 commits, open and self-reviewed. Drift 0, 94% adopted, four exceptions, one check reported as not run. The repository ends with the standard's spec flow as its only spec flow, its principles in one file, and its own agent guards fixed - adopting the standard is what surfaced that those guards were failing open, because an unset environment variable made every hook exit 127 with empty output, which the host treats as non-blocking. The user ends knowing exactly what is left: four capabilities with no spec, a persona roster nobody has confirmed, and one advisory CI job that stays advisory until those exist.

**Where a person would give up:** Not the interview - four questions, all answered in one line. The risk is the 83% report. The agent finished a long unattended stretch, presented a number built on ten exceptions and a written defence of the conflicting tool, and framed it as the outcome. That is a plausible place to stop, accept it, and never learn that 94% and drift 0 were one authorisation away. The second risk is silence: the user asked 'jak idize' mid-run, which is what a person types when they cannot tell a working session from a dead one.

**Why this verdict:** The verdict rests on the run reversing itself under pressure rather than on its final number. The exceptions written in the unattended stretch are checkable against the manifest as it stood then - ten of them, six covering the competing toolchain's own skill files - and against the friction note that argued the standard should accommodate the local layout. The same note in the merged state says the opposite and records who overruled it. The layout guard is the sharpest evidence that the exception route was a dead end rather than a judgment call: it reads the repository's own file list, so its finding could not be excepted away, and the agent had recorded it as permanent drift anyway. On the positive side, the fail-open guard defect is independently checkable - the hooks invoked a path built from an environment variable that is unset in some contexts, and the self-test that now covers it fails against the old wiring.
